Software is the medium through which I express myself. Writing about software, side projects and things I learn along the way.

paras: I build full-stack web apps and AI/ML tools for people who would rather not think about the tech behind them. As an undergrad engineering student, I spend most of my time shipping side projects, experimenting with models, and figuring out how to turn raw ideas into useful software.

I care about the details that make a product actually feel good to use: how fast an API responds, the second a streaming response starts appearing, and making sure the interface stays simple no matter how complex the backend gets.
Outside of classes and coding, I enjoy taking photographs, tinkering with new tools, and writing about what I learn along the way. Driven by curiosity, good coffee, and building things from scratch.

posts.x: Today, on a whim, I went live on YouTube to try Framer Sites and see what all the buzz is about. You can watch the recap here.
posts.body:
Today, on a whim, I went live on YouTube to try Framer Sites and see what all the buzz is about.

## What worked

Going from a blank canvas to a published page took under an hour. The layout primitives feel familiar if you have ever used auto layout, and responsive behavior is mostly predictable.

## What didn’t

Typography controls are thinner than I expected, and exporting design tokens is not possible yet. For a portfolio it is more than enough. For a design system it is not.

posts.t: Design critique for fun and profit
posts.x: Last week I asked Twitter if anyone would pay for visual design critique as a service — I love helping people fix small visual bugs in their designs, but would a business pay for this?
posts.body:
Last week I asked Twitter if anyone would pay for visual design critique as a service — I love helping people fix small visual bugs in their designs, but would a business pay for this?

From that initial tweet, to a quick pricing survey, to a payment link, took just two hours, and then within a day 3 businesses had signed up.

While this series of events may have been a fluke, I promised to share everything I’m learning about this process, outcome included. While I’ve only completed two projects, the tone, price and expectations have changed drastically.

Here’s what I’ve learned so far:

## Never charge by the hour

I knew not to do this, but I still did it. Never charge by the hour.

I don’t want to live my life thinking about the price of a minute, or being distracted by the clock as I try to solve a problem. In my first Crit, the two hour crunch made me feel like I was forced to compromise the quality of the artifact. I chose to go way over time and spent 6 hours on that first project. The extra time helped me end with a result that I can stand behind.

I should have omitted the “two hours” line completely in my tweet. The right move is to charge for the value being delivered. Businesses pay for outcomes and designers shouldn’t be punished for being fast.

## Expectations are hard to correct

Besides framing the Crit as a by-the-hour service, the second biggest mistake I made was framing the offering as a visual design critique only. After working with my first two customers, it’s clear that going below the surface-level look and feel is unavoidable. Visuals are inherently tied to usability, hierarchy, copywriting and navigation.

I’m now in a position where a lot of people assume this service is purely visual. I’ve tried to remedy this by updating the entire landing page to communicate that this service is a comprehensive product design health check. This framing sounds more correct, is easier to communicate, and I think is a more attractive offer for a business anyways.

Interestingly, one customer has explicitly asked that I only focus on their visual design. We’ll see if this is an exception, or something consistently in demand.

posts.x: If you’re like me, you’ve found yourself in a situation where you were so excited to pursue a new goal, start a new side project, or explore a new hobby, that you just couldn’t wait to tell the world.
posts.body:
If you’re like me, you’ve found yourself in a situation where you were so excited to pursue a new goal that you just couldn’t wait to tell the world.

Announcing a project feels like progress. It rarely is. The excitement you get from telling people is the same reward you would have gotten from shipping, and your brain does not tell the difference.

## Ship quietly

These days I keep new projects to myself until there is something a stranger could use. The announcement is the reward for the work, not a substitute for it.

posts.x: My personal website is an over-engineered playground where I can tinker, learn new things, test new tools, break all the rules, and just scratch that itch deep in my brain that wants to understand how the hell web software works.
posts.body:
My personal website is an over-engineered playground where I can tinker, learn new things and break all the rules.

## The stack

Static pages, a small build step and a handful of hand-written components. Every dependency has to earn its place, and most of them don’t.

## Why bother

A portfolio is the one project with no client and no deadline. It is the best place to learn how things actually work.

posts.t: Typing fast is a high-leverage skill
posts.x: Typing fast is the one of the highest leverage skills you can develop in tech. It doesn’t matter if you’re a designer, programmer, PM, or anything else — slow typing disrupts the creative flow.
posts.body:
Typing fast is one of the highest leverage skills you can develop in tech.

It doesn’t matter if you’re a designer, programmer, PM, or anything else — slow typing disrupts the creative flow. When your hands keep up with your thoughts, you stop editing ideas before they reach the page.

## How I practiced

Fifteen minutes a day for a month. Accuracy first, speed second. It paid for itself within weeks.
